the greatest happiness and enjoyment were experienced during leisure time, but that enjoyment was also high in paid work.

enjoyment is a key component of wellbeing in all activity, and is experienced more frequently in leisure than in work, but is experienced equally in leisure and work when the activity involves high challenge and high skill.
enjoyment of paid work and leisure activities is a significant predictor of happiness and that enjoyment of leisure is greater than enjoyment of paid work or life work.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationships between paid and unpaid work and leisure in the context of wellbeing.
the relationships between activity, enjoyment and happiness, which are of increasing interest in the context of the wellbeing debate in education, government and society generally.
the wellbeing of academic staff in a higher education institution.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
paid work is not the enemy of leisure and well-being; it is the quality of activity that is the key to understanding the nature of the experience of paid work and leisure.
paid work is a source of enjoyment and happiness, and leisure is a source of happiness.
paid work, life-work, leisure and wellbeing are interdependent, but that the most significant relationships are between wellbeing and enjoyment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the more we are engaged with our work, the happier we feel, and that this is as true for work as it is for leisure.
the most important factors for wellbeing are enjoyment, interest and happiness.
the more enjoyable the activity, the more happiness.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is not the activity per se that is important, but rather the enjoyment of the activity, and that this enjoyment can be experienced in a variety of settings.
enjoyment and happiness are more likely to occur in activities that are moderately challenging and that require skills.
enjoyment and happiness are more likely to be found in paid work, leisure and life work, and that enjoyment is more likely when skills match moderate or high challenge.
